t.1.64.1: Then, O Rāma, the great sage left the Himalayan region and, reaching the eastern quarter, practised austerities of the most severe kind.
t.1.64.2: Having undertaken the unsurpassed vow of silence for a thousand years, O Rāma, he performed an incomparable austerity, supremely difficult to accomplish.
t.1.64.4: Then the gods, together with the Gandharvas, Pannagas, Asuras and Rākṣasas, bewildered by the splendour of his austerity, their own radiance dimmed, all stricken with dejection, spoke to the Grandfather.
t.1.64.3: When the thousand years were complete, anger did not enter the heart of the great sage, who had become like a piece of wood, though he was assailed by many obstacles.
t.1.64.6: For not the slightest fault is now seen in him. But if what he desires in his mind is not granted to him, he will destroy by his austerity the three worlds with all that moves and does not move.
t.1.64.5: O god, the great sage Viśvāmitra, though tempted and provoked to anger by many means, only grows ever greater through his austerity.
t.1.64.7: All the oceans are agitated, and the mountains are crumbling; the earth trembles, and the wind blows in great turmoil.
t.1.64.8: O god, before the great sage sets his mind on destruction, the blessed one, fire-like in form and of great splendour, must be appeased.
t.1.64.9: The entire three worlds are being burned, as once before by the fire of Time. He may even seek the kingship of the gods; let whatever he desires be granted to him.
t.1.64.10: Then all the hosts of the gods, with the Grandsire at their head, spoke sweet words to the great-souled Viśvāmitra.
t.1.64.11: Welcome to you, O Brahmarṣi; we are well pleased by your austerity. Through fierce austerity you have attained the status of a brāhmaṇa, O Kauśika.
t.1.64.13: Having heard the words of the Grandfather and of all the dwellers of heaven, the great sage, delighted, made obeisance and spoke.
t.1.64.12: Together with the host of Maruts, I give you long life, O brahman. Attain well-being, may good fortune be yours; go, gentle one, as you please.
t.1.64.14: If brahminhood has truly been attained by me, and likewise a long life, then let the sacred syllable Oṃ, the sacrificial call Vaṣaṭ, and the Vedas choose me as their own.
t.1.64.16: Then Vasiṣṭha, the best of those who recite prayers, being appeased by the gods, made friendship with him, and the brahmarṣi said, "So be it."
t.1.64.15: O deities, let Vasiṣṭha, the son of Brahmā, foremost among those who know the Kṣatra-veda and also among those who know the Brahma-veda, address me thus. If this supreme desire of mine is fulfilled, then let the foremost of the gods depart.
t.1.64.17: The status of a brahmarṣi, there is no doubt, all of it will come to pass for you. Having spoken thus, all the deities too went back as they had come.
t.1.64.18: The righteous-souled Viśvāmitra, too, having attained the supreme state of a brāhmaṇa, paid homage to the brahmarṣi Vasiṣṭha, foremost among those who recite prayers.
t.1.64.19: His desire fulfilled, he wandered over the whole earth, steadfast in austerity. Thus, O Rāma, was brahminhood attained by this great-souled one.
t.1.64.20: This man, O Rāma, is the foremost of sages; he is asceticism embodied. He is forever the supreme dharma, and he is the ultimate abode of valor.
t.1.64.21: Having heard the words of Śatānanda, Janaka, with joined palms, spoke these words to the son of Kuśika in the presence of Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa.
t.1.64.23: O Brahman, O great sage, I have been purified by you through the sight of you; from beholding you I have gained manifold blessings.
t.1.64.22: I am blessed, I am favored, O bull among sages, O Kākutstha, for you, O righteous one, have come to my sacrifice with your companions.
t.1.64.24: O Brahman, O greatly radiant one, your great austerity, being recounted in full detail, has been heard by me and by the great-souled Rāma.
t.1.64.25: And when the assembly members had reached the assembly hall, they heard of your many virtues.
t.1.64.26: Immeasurable is your austerity, and immeasurable is your strength; immeasurable, too, are your virtues, always, O son of Kuśika.
t.1.64.27: O lord, I can never have enough of these wondrous tales. But it is now the time for the rites, O best of sages, for the disc of the sun is sinking.
t.1.64.29: Having spoken thus to the foremost of sages, the Vaideha king, lord of Mithilā, together with his preceptors and his kinsmen, quickly circumambulated him.
t.1.64.28: Tomorrow at daybreak, O greatly radiant one, you should see me again. Welcome to you, O best of ascetics; now you should grant me leave to go.
t.1.64.30: Viśvāmitra too, the righteous-souled one, together with Rāma and with Lakṣmaṇa, went to his own enclosure, being honoured by the great sages.
